expected_evidence: Ancient DNA (aDNA) time-series from North American megafauna (mammoth, horse, bison, ground sloth) showing declining effective population size / heterozygosity in the millennia before extinction, temporally aligned with meltwater-pulse dates

Sedimentary and isotopic records (δ18O in corals, speleothems, ice cores; freshwater discharge layers) documenting the timing and magnitude of the meltwater pulse (e.g., MWP-1A ~14.6 ka) for cross-correlation with biological decline
Radiocarbon date-frequency distributions (summed probability distributions) of megafaunal fossils showing a taper/decline in occurrence density coincident with or following the pulse

Sea-level/proglacial lake outburst geological evidence (varves, outwash deposits) establishing the causal hydrological mechanism (AMOC disruption, regional cooling) linking the pulse to ecosystem stress
Paleoecological proxies (pollen, coprophilous fungal spores like Sporormiella) indicating vegetation/habitat shifts and megaherbivore decline in North American basins
Faunal turnover/extinction chronologies from stratified fossil sites bracketing the interval
response.rationale: The hypothesis requires corroboration between a hydrological/climatic event (meltwater pulse) and a demographic decline in megafauna, so the diagnostic evidence classes are genetic (aDNA population-decline signatures), geological (meltwater/outwash/isotopic records dating and characterizing the pulse), and material (radiocarbon-dated fossil abundance and paleoecological proxies like Sporormiella). The interval (-19050 to -9050) spans the Late Upper Paleolithic through the Younger Dryas into the Early Holocene, so I averaged detectability across those three period rows rather than a single bucket. Geological detectability is comparatively strong in this era (0.60–0.65 across the three periods) because meltwater pulses leave robust, independently dateable sedimentary/isotopic signatures that survive well over these timescales. Genetic detectability is weaker and rising through the interval (0.25 → 0.30 → 0.35) since ancient DNA preservation in North American climates is possible but degrades with age and is unevenly sampled across taxa and sites — this is a real limiting factor, not evidence against the hypothesis. Material/fossil evidence (radiocarbon date-frequency, faunal assemblages) sits in the low-to-mid range (0.35–0.45), constrained by preservation bias and dating precision (reservoir effects, hiatuses) rather than absence of the phenomenon. Notably, this is a genuine, actively studied research program in Quaternary science — model-prior recollection (unverified, low-tier) suggests published work (e.g., Lorenzen et al. 2011-style ancient-DNA demographic reconstructions, and separate abrupt-warming/extinction correlation studies) has attempted exactly this kind of multi-proxy corroboration, meaning the evidence types listed are not merely hypothetical but plausibly already exist in the literature to some degree. Given the moderate-to-good detectability of the geological leg and the real but imperfect detectability of the genetic leg, a fully corroborated (all evidence lines aligned) case is achievable but not guaranteed to be fully resolved; a low or missing corroboration signal should not be read as strong evidence against the hypothesis, since genetic and fine-grained demographic data in particular remain only moderately detectable across this multi-period interval.
